learn.hook: A 'Mexican wave' sweeps around a packed Wankhede Stadium, yet no spectator leaves their seat. That's exactly how a wave works.
points: A wave transfers energy and information from one place to another without transporting matter as a whole.

Mechanical waves (sound, waves on strings, water waves, seismic waves) need a material medium. Electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays) do not need a medium. Matter waves are associated with moving particles like electrons.
In a mechanical wave, each particle of the medium only oscillates about its mean position; it is the disturbance (pattern) that travels.
Wave propagation needs two properties of the medium: elasticity (restoring forces between neighbouring parts) and inertia (mass) of its parts.

example.q: A paper boat floats on a pond as ripples pass. Does it move along with the ripples?
steps: The ripples carry energy across the water.
Each water particle, and the boat on it, just moves up and down (and slightly to and fro) about its place.
So the boat bobs but is not carried along by the wave.
example.answer: No, it only bobs about its position

learn.reallife: Mobile phone signals, Doordarshan broadcasts and the light from the Sun are electromagnetic waves; they travel even through the vacuum of space.

A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Without particles there is nothing to oscillate. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sound is an electromagnetic wave

teach.ask: Gappu thinks waves in the pond carry water from one side to the other. Explain what a wave really transfers and what a medium does.
teach.praise: The water just bobs; the wave carries energy across. Mechanical waves need a medium, light does not!
teach.nudge: Does the water travel with the wave? What does the wave carry?

learn.hook: During an earthquake, the first jolt (P-wave) squeezes and stretches the ground; the later, more destructive shaking (S-wave) moves it side to side.
points: Transverse waves: particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation (wave on a string, ripples on a stretched rope).
Longitudinal waves: particles oscillate along the direction of propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions (sound in air, P-waves).

Transverse mechanical waves need the medium to resist shear (shear modulus), so they travel in solids and along strings, but not through the bulk of liquids or gases. Longitudinal waves travel in solids, liquids and gases.
Water surface waves are a combination of both: water particles move in roughly circular paths.
Classify by asking: do particles move across (transverse) or along (longitudinal) the direction the wave travels?

example.q: Classify: (a) sound from a sitar in air (b) the vibration of the sitar string (c) ripples on a lake.
steps: (a) Air particles oscillate along the direction of travel: longitudinal.
(b) The string vibrates perpendicular to its length: transverse.
(c) Water particles move in circles: both transverse and longitudinal.

learn.reallife: Seismologists at NCS (National Center for Seismology) use the arrival gap between P-waves and S-waves to locate earthquake epicentres.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks sound in air shakes up and down like a skipping rope. Explain transverse and longitudinal waves and where each can travel.
teach.praise: Rope waves move across, sound waves squeeze along! Transverse needs shear, so not through air or water.
teach.nudge: Which way do particles move in each kind of wave? Why can't air carry transverse waves?

learn.hook: One compact equation, y = a sin(kx − ωt + φ), describes the wave on a sitar string at every point and every instant.
points: A sinusoidal wave travelling in +x: y(x, t) = a sin(kx − ωt + φ). In −x: y = a sin(kx + ωt + φ).
a = amplitude (maximum displacement). (kx − ωt + φ) = phase; φ = phase constant (initial phase at x = 0, t = 0).
Wavelength λ: distance between two consecutive points in the same phase (e.g. crests). Angular wave number k = 2π/λ (unit rad m⁻¹).
Period T: time for one oscillation of a particle; angular frequency ω = 2π/T; frequency ν = 1/T = ω/2π.
Reading a wave equation: match it with a sin(kx − ωt + φ) and identify a, k, ω, then λ = 2π/k, T = 2π/ω.

example.q: y = 0.005 sin(80x − 3t) (SI units). Find amplitude, wavelength, period and frequency.

learn.reallife: Engineers at All India Radio describe carrier waves by equations of exactly this form, with frequencies of hundreds of kHz.

teach.praise: a is the amplitude, λ = 2π/k, ν = ω/2π, and kx − ωt means it travels towards +x!
teach.nudge: Which number is the amplitude? How do you get λ and ν from k and ω? Which way does it travel?

topics.title: Wave speed and waves on strings

learn.hook: Tighten a sitar string and the note rises. Higher tension makes waves travel faster along the string.
points: Following a point of constant phase (kx − ωt = constant) gives the wave speed v = ω/k = λ/T = νλ.
Wave speed depends on the properties of the medium (elasticity and inertia), not on the frequency of the source. Changing the source frequency changes λ, not v.
Transverse wave on a stretched string: v = √(T/μ), where T is the tension and μ the mass per unit length. Dimensional analysis gives this form (constant = 1 from full theory).
Example: a wire of μ = 0.01 kg m⁻¹ under 100 N tension carries waves at √(100/0.01) = 100 m s⁻¹.

example.q: A 2 m wire of mass 0.04 kg is stretched with a tension of 50 N. Find the speed of a transverse pulse and the time to cross the wire.

learn.reallife: Sitar and veena players tune strings by adjusting tension with the pegs: v = √(T/μ) sets the pitch.

games.title: Finding the speed of a pulse on a wire
items: For time to cross, divide length by v

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true (larger μ). R is false: v = √(T/μ) depends on tension.

teach.ask: Gappu tightens a vine and the twang sounds higher. Explain wave speed, v = νλ, and the speed on a stretched string.
teach.praise: Tighter vine, faster waves: v = √(T/μ). And speed is set by the medium, not the source!
teach.nudge: What two properties of a string set the wave speed? Does changing frequency change the speed?

topics.title: Speed of sound: Newton's formula and Laplace's correction

learn.hook: Put your ear to a railway track and you hear the train long before the sound comes through the air. Sound is much faster in steel.
points: Speed of longitudinal waves: v = √(B/ρ) in a fluid (B = bulk modulus), v = √(Y/ρ) in a solid rod.
Sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases (e.g. roughly 5000 m s⁻¹ in steel, 1500 m s⁻¹ in water, 340 m s⁻¹ in air).
Newton assumed isothermal compressions: B = P, giving v = √(P/ρ) ≈ 280 m s⁻¹ for air at STP, about 15% too low.
Laplace correction: compressions are fast and adiabatic, so B = γP and v = √(γP/ρ). With γ = 1.4 for air, v ≈ 331 m s⁻¹ at 0 °C, matching experiment.
v ∝ √T (absolute temperature). At constant temperature, changing pressure does not change v (since P/ρ stays constant).

example.q: Using Newton's formula, the speed of sound in air at STP comes out as 280 m s⁻¹. What does Laplace's correction give (γ = 1.4, √1.4 ≈ 1.183)?

learn.reallife: In a Rajasthan summer at 47 °C, sound travels noticeably faster than on a cold Shimla winter morning, because v ∝ √T.

games.title: Speed of sound in air: theory sequence

Assertion (A): The speed of sound in air increases when the air pressure is increased at constant temperature.

teach.ask: Gappu says, 'Newton must have been right about the speed of sound.' Explain Newton's formula, Laplace's correction and how temperature and pressure affect v.
teach.praise: Newton used isothermal and got 280 m/s; Laplace used adiabatic (γP) and got 331 m/s! And v ∝ √T.
teach.nudge: What assumption did Newton make? How did Laplace fix it? What changes v: temperature or pressure?

topics.title: Using sound speed, and the superposition principle

learn.hook: During a monsoon storm, count the seconds between the lightning flash and the thunder, multiply by 340, and you know how far the strike was.
points: Echo: sound travels to the reflector and back, so distance d = vt/2.
Lightning–thunder: light arrives almost instantly, so distance ≈ v_sound × delay.
Principle of superposition: when two or more waves overlap, the net displacement at a point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements: y = y₁ + y₂ + ….
Two pulses moving in opposite directions pass through each other and emerge unchanged; while overlapping, they add (a crest and an equal trough momentarily cancel).

example.q: A girl shouts in front of a cliff and hears the echo after 2 s (v = 340 m s⁻¹). How far is the cliff?
steps: Sound goes to the cliff and back: total path = vt = 340 × 2 = 680 m.

learn.reallife: Bats over the forests of the Western Ghats use echoes to locate insects, timing returns to fractions of a millisecond.

items.q: Echo after 1 s: distance to wall (m)
y₁ = 3 mm, y₂ = −1 mm: net y (mm)

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

teach.ask: Gappu counted 3 seconds between a lightning flash and thunder. Teach him to find the distance, then explain superposition of waves.
teach.praise: About 1 km away! Echoes need a ÷2, and overlapping waves just add their displacements.
teach.nudge: How do you find the distance from the thunder delay? What happens when two waves overlap?

learn.hook: Noise-cancelling headphones play a sound wave exactly opposite to the outside noise. The two add up to near silence.
points: Two waves of the same frequency and amplitude a, travelling in the same direction with phase difference φ: y₁ = a sin(kx − ωt), y₂ = a sin(kx − ωt + φ).
Resultant: y = 2a cos(φ/2) sin(kx − ωt + φ/2). The resultant amplitude is A = 2a cos(φ/2).
Constructive interference: φ = 0 (or 2nπ), A = 2a (intensity 4 times one wave).
Destructive interference: φ = π (or (2n + 1)π), A = 0.
Intermediate phases give amplitudes between 0 and 2a (e.g. φ = 2π/3 gives A = a).

example.q: Two waves of amplitude 3 mm and the same frequency travel together with a phase difference of π/2. Find the resultant amplitude.

learn.reallife: Concert halls like NCPA Mumbai are designed to avoid dead spots where reflected sound waves interfere destructively.

Assertion (A): Two waves of equal amplitude and frequency can cancel each other completely.
Reason (R): Two waves of equal amplitude always have equal frequencies.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: A is true (phase difference π). R is false: amplitude and frequency are independent.

teach.ask: Gappu and a friend chirp the same note; sometimes it gets louder, sometimes nearly silent. Explain interference.
teach.praise: In phase, the amplitude doubles; out of phase by π, they cancel. A = 2a cos(φ/2) covers everything in between!
teach.nudge: What decides whether two waves reinforce or cancel? What is the resultant amplitude formula?

learn.hook: Shake a rope tied to a wall at just the right rate and it forms a still pattern of loops. Waves going and coming back create a standing wave.
points: Reflection at a rigid boundary (fixed end): the reflected wave has a phase change of π, so a crest returns as a trough (pulse inverted).
Reflection at an open (free) boundary: no phase change; a crest returns as a crest.
The incident and reflected waves superpose to form a standing (stationary) wave: y = 2a sin kx cos ωt.
Nodes: points of zero amplitude (sin kx = 0): x = nλ/2. Antinodes: points of maximum amplitude 2a: x = (n + ½)λ/2.
Distance between adjacent nodes (or adjacent antinodes) = λ/2; between a node and the next antinode = λ/4.

example.q: A standing wave on a string has adjacent nodes 20 cm apart. Find the wavelength and the distance between a node and the nearest antinode.
steps: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart: λ = 40 cm.
Node to next antinode = λ/4 = 10 cm.

learn.reallife: Tabla and mridangam skins vibrate in standing-wave patterns; the black syahi patch shapes these modes to give their rich tones.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Zero displacement means no energy flow through a node. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu ties a vine to a tree, shakes it and sees still loops. Explain reflection at boundaries and the formation of standing waves.
teach.praise: The reflected wave meets the incoming one, making nodes (no motion) and antinodes (big motion), λ/2 apart!
teach.nudge: What happens to a wave reflected from a fixed end? How far apart are neighbouring nodes?

topics.title: Normal modes of strings and air columns

learn.hook: A flute and a clarinet can play the same note, but they sound different. One is open at both ends, the other closed at one: different harmonics.
points: String fixed at both ends (nodes at both ends): λₙ = 2L/n, νₙ = nv/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, … The lowest (n = 1) is the fundamental; all harmonics are present.
Air column closed at one end (node at closed end, antinode at open end): L = (2n − 1)λ/4, νₙ = (2n − 1)v/(4L). Only odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) are present.
Air column open at both ends (antinodes at both ends): νₙ = nv/(2L); all harmonics are present.
For the same length, the fundamental of a closed pipe (v/4L) is half that of an open pipe (v/2L).

example.q: A string 0.5 m long carries waves at 200 m s⁻¹. Find the fundamental and the next two harmonics.

learn.hook: In the CBSE physics lab, you lower a glass tube in water while a tuning fork hums above it. Suddenly it booms: resonance!
points: Resonance tube: an air column closed at the bottom by water. With a fork of frequency ν, resonance occurs when L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4, …
Successive resonance lengths differ by λ/2: L₂ − L₁ = λ/2, so v = 2ν(L₂ − L₁). This removes the error of the end correction.
Harmonic numericals: for strings ν = nv/(2L) with v = √(T/μ); for closed pipes ν = (2n − 1)v/(4L); for open pipes ν = nv/(2L).
Check which harmonics are allowed before answering (e.g. a closed pipe can't give 2ν₁).

example.q: With a 500 Hz fork, resonances occur at 16.5 cm and 50.5 cm. Find the speed of sound.
steps: L₂ − L₁ = 34 cm = λ/2, so λ = 68 cm = 0.68 m.

learn.reallife: Resonance-tube experiments in Indian school labs routinely give the speed of sound within a few percent of 340 m s⁻¹. Lab safety: strike the tuning fork only on a rubber pad (never on the glass tube or the bench), and handle the glass tube gently to avoid breakage.

In a resonance tube, the difference between two successive resonance lengths equals
quiz.explain: From L = λ/4 to 3λ/4.

quiz.q: A string 1.5 m long (both ends fixed) carries waves at 300 m s⁻¹. Its third harmonic in Hz is
A closed pipe has fundamental 120 Hz. Which frequency (in Hz) can it NOT produce?
quiz.explain: Only odd multiples of 120 Hz: 360, 600, 840 Hz are allowed; 240 Hz is an even multiple.

quiz.q: A steel wire of length 0.5 m, μ = 0.01 kg m⁻¹, tension 100 N, is fixed at both ends. Its fundamental frequency in Hz is
An open pipe resonates at successive frequencies 400 Hz and 500 Hz. Its fundamental frequency in Hz is
quiz.explain: Open pipes have all harmonics: the difference of successive harmonics = ν₁ = 100 Hz.

quiz.q: A closed pipe resonates at successive frequencies 750 Hz and 1050 Hz. Its fundamental frequency in Hz is
quiz.explain: Successive odd harmonics differ by 2ν₁: 300 = 2ν₁ → ν₁ = 150 Hz.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Using the difference of two resonance lengths gives a more accurate speed of sound than using the first length alone.
Reason (R): The end correction cancels out when one resonance length is subtracted from another.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both lengths share the same end correction, which disappears in L₂ − L₁. R explains A.

teach.ask: Gappu did the resonance-tube experiment and got two loud lengths. Teach him to find the speed of sound and to solve harmonic problems.
teach.praise: The gap between resonances is λ/2, so v = 2ν(L₂ − L₁). And closed pipes only allow odd harmonics!
teach.nudge: What does the difference between two resonance lengths equal? How do you get v from it?

learn.hook: When two harmonium reeds are slightly out of tune, you hear a 'wah-wah-wah' throbbing. Those are beats.
points: Beats: periodic rise and fall (waxing and waning) of loudness heard when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies superpose.
Beat frequency = number of beats per second = |ν₁ − ν₂|.
Musicians tune instruments by sounding a note with a standard and adjusting until the beats disappear.

Unknown fork: if fork B gives n beats with a known fork A (ν_A), then ν_B = ν_A ± n. Loading B with wax lowers ν_B; filing its prongs raises ν_B. Watch whether beats increase or decrease to choose the sign.
Mixed numericals: read wave equations, standing waves on strings, organ pipes and beats.

example.q: A 512 Hz fork A gives 5 beats s⁻¹ with fork B. When B is loaded with a little wax, the beats fall to 3 s⁻¹. Find ν_B.
steps: Wax lowers ν_B. If ν_B = 517, it moves towards 512 and beats decrease ✓. If 507, beats would increase ✗.

learn.reallife: Sitar players tuning to a tanpura listen for beats; when the throbbing stops, the strings are in unison.

games.title: Finding an unknown fork's frequency by beats
items: Sound the unknown fork with a known fork and count beats per second, n
Write the two possibilities: ν_known ± n
Load (or file) the unknown fork slightly
Count beats again and see if they increase or decrease
Choose the value consistent with the change

items.q: ν₁ = 300 Hz, 5 beats/s, ν₂ > ν₁: ν₂ (Hz)

quiz.q: Two tuning forks of 384 Hz and 388 Hz are sounded together. The number of beats per second is
quiz.explain: Beat frequency = 388 − 384 = 4 Hz.

quiz.q: A 256 Hz fork gives 4 beats s⁻¹ with an unknown fork. Filing the unknown fork (raising its frequency) increases the beats. The unknown frequency in Hz was
quiz.explain: If it were 260, raising it moves away from 256: beats increase ✓. If 252, beats would first decrease.

quiz.q: A 480 Hz fork gives 6 beats s⁻¹ with fork X. Loading X with wax increases the beats. ν_X in Hz was
quiz.explain: Wax lowers ν_X; beats increase only if ν_X was below 480, i.e. 474 Hz.

quiz.q: Beats are heard when two sound waves
quiz.explain: The slow drifting phase difference makes loudness rise and fall.

quiz.q: Musicians tune an instrument to a reference by
quiz.explain: Zero beats means equal frequencies.
quiz.mistake: Thinks more beats means better tuning

quiz.q: 20 beats are heard in 5 s between two sources. If one is 500 Hz, the other could be (in Hz)
quiz.explain: Beat frequency = 20/5 = 4 Hz → 504 or 496 Hz; 504 is among the options.

quiz.q: Loading a prong of a tuning fork with wax
quiz.explain: Extra mass lowers the natural frequency.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two sitar strings slightly out of tune produce a throbbing sound when plucked together.
Reason (R): Waves on plucked strings are transverse.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the throbbing is explained by beats from slightly different frequencies, not by the wave being transverse.
quiz.mistake: Picks a true but irrelevant fact

teach.ask: Gappu hears a 'wah-wah' when he and his sister hum nearly the same note. Explain beats and how to use them to find an unknown frequency.
teach.praise: The throb rate is the difference of frequencies! Tune until the beats vanish, and use wax or filing to solve fork puzzles.
teach.nudge: What causes beats? How is the beat frequency related to the two frequencies?
